core.title: Keep plan-forbidden properties out of emit calls
core.given: After adoption, an emit-like call (a telemetry emit that names a declared concrete tracking-plan item id) that supplies the call's properties; how the call names the id and carries its properties is the profile's telemetry emit idiom.
core.when: The call exists or changes, or the named item's forbidden_properties list or the call's item id changes.
core.then: No top-level named property of the call's properties MAY match a property the plan forbids on that item, compared after stripping separators and folding case (property entries that carry no name of their own are not scanned; nested property groups are judged at their own level).
prefer: Pass the identifier, not the thing it identifies, and leave out any property the named item's plan forbids.
avoid: Attaching raw payloads, secrets or prompts the plan forbids on the named item.
Evading the check by renaming case/separators (snake_case vs camelCase) instead of removing the property.
Treating properties the plan merely does not declare as forbidden or removing them for this rule; undeclared-key drift is the generated contract's concern.
unless: The call names an id the registry does not hold: that is the raw-string rule's finding; double-reporting here would be noise.
Inert until adoption, like every rule in this family.
core.why: The forbidden list is a privacy and cost promise, so it is enforced where data leaves: the emit call itself, against the plan entry the call names.
evidence: The telemetry-code check reports no forbidden-property finding for emit-like calls naming declared items.
For every emit call naming a declared item (not only changed ones), every normalized top-level property of the call's properties is absent from that item's forbidden_properties list.
verification: Scope: only emit-like calls that name a declared concrete id in the tracking-plan registry, recognized by the profile's telemetry emit idiom; calls naming an id the registry does not hold are skipped (the raw-string rule reports them). All qualifying calls are checked after adoption, regardless of whether the call itself changed.
Properties: the named properties supplied with the emit-like call, in whatever shape the profile's telemetry emit idiom recognizes; only their top-level named entries are compared.
forbidden_property: a name in the item's forbidden_properties list (raw payloads, secrets, prompts): what must never leave the process on that item.

Normalization: every top-level property name has separators stripped and case folded before comparison against the item's forbidden list; the plan and the code may use different naming conventions (e.g. snake_case in the plan, camelCase in the code).
Property entries that carry no name of their own are invisible to this scan; nested property groups are judged at their own level, not as top-level entries of this call.
Properties the plan merely does not declare are not forbidden by this rule; undeclared-key drift is the generated contract's concern, not this rule's.
The check is realized as a telemetry-source code validator; the detector, validator and finding ids of this rule are realization details of each stack.
Disposition: strict — the check fails on every finding; no advisory mode and no ratchet baseline. Severity: 3.

fires: After adoption, any emit-like call names a declared tracking-plan item and a top-level property of its properties is in that item's forbidden_properties list (e.g. a raw payload, secret or prompt).
The plan forbids a snake_case name and the code writes the same name in camelCase as a top-level property of the call's properties.
A plan change adds a name to an item's forbidden_properties list that an existing, unchanged emit call already passes.
A call's named item id is changed to an item whose forbidden list contains one of the call's existing keys.
doesNotFire: The emit-like call names an id the registry does not hold (that is the raw-string rule's finding).
The call's properties carry a name the plan merely does not declare (undeclared-key drift belongs to the generated contract).
The value is passed via a property entry that carries no name of its own, which this scan cannot see.
A matching name appears only inside a nested property group (nested groups are judged at their own level, not as top-level properties of this call).
The repository has not yet adopted the tracking plan.

neutralityNotes: The obligation itself is stack-neutral: telemetry emit calls, the tracking plan's forbidden_properties list, normalized top-level property comparison, the adoption gate, and the raw-string/generated-contract boundaries name no stack. Per the round-2 audit, the concrete properties syntax is delegated to the profile: the core speaks only of an emit-like call naming a declared item and the named properties it supplies, while the argument position (first argument is the id) and the object-literal-on-the-same-statement shape live in the proposed idiom.telemetry#telemetry_emit_call key's Bun value, so another stack (e.g. one that builds properties without an object literal) can supply its own equivalent. 'Shorthand properties' is generalized to 'property entries that carry no name of their own' and 'nested objects' to 'nested property groups'. Kept Bun-specific: the validator and finding ids (bun_telemetry_code, bun_telemetry_code:forbidden-property) and the concrete telemetry.emit fix example. The 'language' activation fact became the neutral file_kind fact 'source', with the concrete languages supplied by the profile (tooling.languages). bun.json gives no source-root or exclusion list for this rule, so no roots requirement was invented.
